title: Productive cough and fever four days after hospital discharge
desc: This station is a focused acute cough history and respiratory examination of a 68-year-old retired teacher in general practice. Four days ago he was discharged from hospital after investigations for chest pain. He now has 2 days of cough with offensive yellow sputum, high fevers, breathlessness and right pleuritic chest pain. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, chest X-ray and bloods (including a D-dimer). They recognise right lower lobe pneumonia acquired around his hospital stay, exclude pulmonary embolism, score severity with CURB-65, arrange admission, answer his COVID worry and safety-net.
focus: Acute productive cough after a recent hospital stay: a history that separates pneumonia from PE and heart failure, then interpreting results, scoring severity and deciding on admission
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your general practice placement. Timothy Reid is a 68-year-old man who has come to the practice with a cough. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first. The GP is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Reid and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, the report of his chest X-ray and his blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Timothy Reid, a 68-year-old retired teacher. You feel awful: hot, shivery and worn out. You cough every few minutes and sometimes have to stop mid-sentence, but you can speak in full sentences. A deep breath makes you wince and hold the right side of your chest. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I've had a bad cough in the past few days and have been coughing up stuff recently."

The cough (give only when asked):

  • Onset: it started suddenly 2 days ago. It has stayed about the same since. You have never had a cough like this before.
  • Sputum: yellow, and it smells bad. About a teaspoon each time. No blood, and it is not pink or frothy.
  • Frequency: you cough about every 5 minutes through the day. It does not wake you at night.
  • Position: no different lying down.

The recent hospital stay (only if asked about recent illness, hospital or tests):

  • Last week you were admitted to the local hospital to investigate chest pain. You went in 8 days ago and were sent home 4 days ago. "They did heart tracings, blood tests and an X-ray and found nothing wrong."
  • The chest pain then was a pressure in the middle of your chest. It has not come back. You have a stress test booked in a week.
  • In hospital you walked around the ward every day. You had a blood-thinning injection in your belly every day, which stopped when you went home.
  • You did not have antibiotics in hospital.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Feeling unwell: you feel terrible, completely washed out.
  • Fever: high fevers since the cough started, with shaking chills last night.
  • Breathlessness: short of breath walking around the house since yesterday, and a little even sitting still.
  • Chest pain: since yesterday, a sharp pain low on the right side of your chest, about 5 out of 10. It catches when you breathe in deeply or cough. It is nothing like the pressure that took you to hospital and it does not spread anywhere.
  • Eating and drinking: you have not felt like eating, and you have been drinking less than usual.

Negatives (only if asked directly):

  • Legs and clots: no calf pain or swelling. No coughing up blood. No fainting or feeling faint. No palpitations. You have never had a clot and have never had cancer.
  • Heart: no breathlessness lying flat, no waking up gasping at night, no ankle swelling, no pink frothy phlegm. The central chest pressure has not come back.
  • Airways: no wheeze. No asthma or COPD. No chest infections in the past, and no daily phlegm before this.
  • Nose and throat: no sore throat, runny nose, earache or sinus pain.
  • Other features: no headache, no diarrhoea, no aching muscles beyond feeling generally unwell. You are not confused.
  • Exposures: no recent work with potting mix or gardening, no spas, and you have not been near air-conditioning cooling towers. No overseas or interstate travel. Your wife is well. No one around you has been sick, and you have not been in contact with anyone with COVID that you know of.
  • Choking: no choking on food or drink, no trouble swallowing, no vomiting, no blackouts or episodes of being very drunk.

Past medical history: tonsils out at 10 and appendix out at 30. No COPD, no asthma, no known heart problems.

Medications: no regular medications. The injections stopped when you left hospital. You have not taken anything for the cough except a couple of paracetamol.

Allergies: peanuts. You had anaphylaxis to peanuts. You have no allergies to any medicines.

Family history: your father died of prostate cancer at 75. Your mother is alive and has type 2 diabetes. You have no brothers or sisters. No one in your family has had blood clots or lung problems.

Social history:

  • You have never smoked.
  • You drink 2 glasses of wine every night, normal-sized glasses of about 150 mL.
  • You are a retired teacher. You live with your wife of 30 years. You have 3 children and 4 grandchildren.
  • You walk about 1 km once a week and eat a balanced diet.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are worried this is COVID. You were going to see the grandchildren on the weekend and don't want to give it to them. You expect a test and something to get rid of the cough. You would rather not go back into hospital so soon.

Question to raise: if the candidate has not asked about your worries by the end of the history, ask: "Is this COVID, doctor?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: unwell-looking, flushed and warm to touch. Coughs often and is mildly short of breath at rest, speaking in full sentences. Not cyanosed. Alert and fully oriented (Abbreviated Mental Test 10/10). Weight 82 kg.
  • Vital signs (10:15): temperature 38.6 °C; HR 104 beats/min regular; BP 128/76 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 94% on room air.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds.
  • Sputum pot: about a teaspoon of thick yellow-green sputum with an offensive smell. No blood.
  • Hands: warm, no clubbing, no flap.
  • Head and neck: throat normal, no cervical lymph nodes. Trachea midline. JVP not raised.
  • Chest: expansion reduced at the right base. Percussion dull over the right lower zone posteriorly, resonant elsewhere. Bronchial breath sounds with coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the right lower zone posteriorly. Left lung clear. No wheeze, no pleural rub.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual with no murmurs or added sounds. No ankle or sacral oedema.
  • 12-lead ECG (only if requested; done by the practice nurse): sinus tachycardia 104/min, normal axis, normal intervals, no ST-segment or T-wave changes (no acute ischaemic change).
  • Legs: both calves soft and non-tender, the same size, with no swelling, redness or warmth.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender. A few small fading bruises from the injections. Well-healed appendicectomy scar.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a final-year medical student, confirms the patient's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation and gains consent.
Takes respiratory precautions for an acute febrile cough: puts on a surgical mask and offers one to Mr Reid.
Opens with an open question, then focuses. Uses plain language and responds with empathy to how unwell he feels and to his COVID worry.
History
Characterises the cough:

kids.x: Onset and course: sudden onset 2 days ago, unchanged since, never had this before.
Sputum and haemoptysis: purulent (yellow), offensive-smelling, no blood, no pink froth.
kids.d: Volume (about a teaspoon each time) is optional and not required for this item.

kids.x: Pattern: coughs about every 5 minutes, not woken at night, no change lying down.

check.x: Asks about recent illness or hospital admission. Finds that he was admitted to investigate chest pain, nothing abnormal was found, he was discharged 4 days ago, and he has a stress test booked in a week.
check.d: This is the key context for both pneumonia acquired in hospital and PE. It is only given if the candidate asks about recent illness, hospital or tests.

check.x: Asks about the features of pneumonia:
check.d: Credit each sub-item when the candidate elicits the listed features; productive cough is credited under item 6.

kids.x: Severe malaise, high fevers and shaking chills.
Breathlessness on walking around the house since yesterday, and a little at rest.
Chest pain: sharp, low on the right, worse on deep breathing and coughing (pleuritic), and different from the pain that led to his admission.

check.x: Screens for pulmonary embolism: calf pain or swelling, haemoptysis, fainting, and VTE risk factors (mobility in hospital, the daily blood-thinning injections (presumed enoxaparin prophylaxis), previous clots, cancer).
check.d: Credit if the candidate asks about leg swelling or pain, haemoptysis, and at least two VTE risk factors (mobility or prophylaxis in hospital, previous clot, cancer).

check.x: Screens for the other causes of an acute cough:
check.d: Credit each condition screened with at least two of the listed questions.

kids.x: Left heart failure or cardiac pain: pink frothy sputum, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling, and whether the admission chest pain has come back (none).
Airways disease: wheeze, known asthma or COPD, smoking, previous chest infections or chronic daily sputum suggesting bronchiectasis (none).
Upper respiratory infection: sore throat, runny nose, ear or sinus pain (none).
Atypical pneumonia: headache, muscle aches, diarrhoea or confusion, and exposure to potting mix, spas or cooling towers (none).
Infectious contacts and aspiration: travel, sick or COVID contacts, choking, swallowing problems, vomiting or blackouts (none).

check.x: Takes the past medical, medication and allergy history:

kids.x: Past history: tonsillectomy at 10, appendicectomy at 30, no COPD or other lung disease.
Medications: none regular. Asks what was started or stopped in hospital (daily blood-thinning injection stopped at discharge, no antibiotics).
Allergies: peanut anaphylaxis. Confirms he has no drug allergies.

check.x: Takes a brief family history (no relevant lung or clotting history).
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Never smoked. Quantifies alcohol: 2 glasses (about 150 mL) of wine every night, roughly 3 standard drinks a day.
Social situation: lives with his wife and is independent; asks about contact with grandchildren (relevant to his concern).

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: worried it is COVID and about infecting his grandchildren, expects a test and treatment, and would rather not go back to hospital.
Examination
General inspection: how unwell he looks, work of breathing, ability to speak in sentences, cyanosis. Checks for new confusion (alert and oriented, AMT 10/10).
Requests a full set of vital signs and identifies fever 38.6 °C, HR 104, RR 22 and SpO2 94% on room air, with a normal blood pressure.
Inspects the sputum (purulent yellow-green, offensive, no blood) and assesses hydration (dry mucous membranes).

Examines the chest front and back (expansion, percussion, auscultation, vocal resonance). Finds signs of consolidation at the right lower zone: reduced expansion, dullness, bronchial breathing, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance.
Looks for heart failure: JVP, heart sounds and murmurs, ankle and sacral oedema (all normal).
check.d: Optional: credit a request for a 12-lead ECG (sinus tachycardia 104, no acute ischaemic change).

check.x: Examines both calves for swelling, tenderness, redness and warmth (normal).
Examines the throat and cervical lymph nodes (normal) and the hands for clubbing (none).
Interpretation
Observations: febrile, with HR and RR rising and SpO2 falling to 91% on room air over the day; BP preserved and alert. States he is deteriorating, needs oxygen and cannot be managed at home.
check.d: Exact starting and finishing numbers are not required.

check.x: Chest X-ray: new right lower lobe consolidation (air bronchograms), not present on the normal film 8 days ago, with no effusion or cavitation and no features of heart failure (normal heart size, no oedema).

Bloods: neutrophil leucocytosis (WCC 16.4) and CRP 168 point to bacterial infection. Urea 8.4 is up from 5.6 at discharge with a normal creatinine, suggesting dehydration. Sodium and liver enzymes are normal (albumin mildly low at 33), so there is no hyponatraemia or liver enzyme rise to suggest Legionella, though this does not exclude it.
check.d: Credit wherever it appears in Part 2 (ISBAR or diagnosis answer); the Legionella comment is optional.

check.x: PE: Wells score 1.5 (HR over 100 only), so PE is unlikely. The D-dimer of 0.58 mg/L is below his age-adjusted cut-off of 0.68 mg/L, so PE is excluded without CTPA, and the X-ray gives a clear alternative diagnosis.
check.d: Also accept a Wells score of 3 if the candidate counts the admission as immobilisation; strictly it does not score because he walked daily, but the score is still 4 or less (PE unlikely) and the D-dimer reasoning stands. A candidate who calls the D-dimer positive and orders a CTPA without applying the age-adjusted cut-off does not earn this item.

check.x: Scores severity: CURB-65 of 2 (age 65 or over, urea above 7 mmol/L; not confused, RR below 30, BP normal), which is moderate severity and warrants hospital care. May also note CORB 0 (SpO2 above 90%).
check.d: Credit in the ISBAR, diagnosis or management answer. The criteria must be named and applied to him.

check.x: States that the most likely diagnosis is right lower lobe bacterial pneumonia acquired around his recent hospital stay (hospital-acquired pneumonia). Justifies it with symptoms starting 2 days after discharge, purulent sputum, fever and rigors, pleuritic pain, right basal consolidation signs, neutrophilia and the new consolidation on X-ray.
check.d: Also accept community-acquired pneumonia as the leading diagnosis if the candidate names the recent hospital stay and says it affects the choice of antibiotics.

check.x: Gives the differentials with a feature against each: community-acquired or atypical pneumonia, PE, acute heart failure or ACS, viral LRTI including COVID-19, and aspiration pneumonia or lung abscess (offensive sputum, but no cavitation).
check.d: Credit any three differentials, each with a feature against it.

check.x: Management
Starts oxygen now by nasal prongs, titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%, sits him up, and repeats observations frequently while he waits.

Arranges same-day admission. With the supervising GP, phones the ED or medical registrar with an ISBAR handover, arranges an ambulance, and sends a referral letter with the results and the recent discharge summary.
States he should not be sent home on oral antibiotics, because of CURB-65 of 2, falling saturations, dehydration and the recent hospital stay. States that a CTPA is not needed.

Hospital plan: blood cultures x2, sputum culture and respiratory viral PCR (SARS-CoV-2, influenza) without delaying antibiotics; ECG (and troponin in hospital); prompt empirical antibiotics per eTG hospital-acquired pneumonia: non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia on clinical judgement (no septic shock, no need for ventilatory or ICU support; CORB 0 supports this) with no multidrug-resistant organism risk (4-day stay, no recent antibiotics), so amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally 12-hourly (IV alternative per eTG if he cannot take oral); piperacillin+tazobactam IV is reserved for severe disease or multidrug-resistant risk; IV fluids. Peanut allergy does not restrict the choice.
check.d: Naming amoxicillin+clavulanate orally with the reason for not choosing piperacillin+tazobactam earns the item; the exact dose is not required. Accept piperacillin+tazobactam if the candidate argues he is severe because of sepsis with organ dysfunction. A candidate who goes straight to piperacillin+tazobactam without a reason does not earn this item. Optional credit: considers sepsis (infection with tachycardia, tachypnoea and new hypoxaemia) and, if ambulance transfer will be delayed, discusses giving the first antibiotic dose in the practice with the registrar (e.g. the first dose of amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally if he can swallow, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM if not, as agreed with the registrar). Also accept the eTG moderate-severity CAP regimen (benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly plus doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly, or the eTG alternative) if the candidate has treated this as CAP under item 29 and says the recent admission was considered and discussed with the registrar.

check.x: Explains in plain language:

kids.x: He has an infection at the bottom of the right lung (pneumonia), probably caught around the time of his hospital stay, and needs hospital for oxygen, a drip and antibiotics. Acknowledges his reluctance and checks his understanding.

COVID: the X-ray and bloods point to a bacterial chest infection, but COVID cannot be ruled out without a swab, which the hospital will do. He should wear a mask and keep away from the grandchildren until the result is back.

check.x: Safety netting

Gives specific red flags in plain words. While waiting: tell the nurse or doctor straight away if he is more breathless, drowsy or has worse chest pain. After discharge: call 000 for worsening breathlessness, blue lips, new confusion or drowsiness, fainting, coughing up blood, or new or worse chest pain; see the GP the same day for returning fevers, not eating or drinking, or a cough not improving.
check.d: Credit at least three red flags with 000 as the action after discharge.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review within a week of discharge, a repeat chest X-ray at about 6 weeks to confirm the consolidation has cleared, postpones and rebooks the stress test and informs cardiology, and checks vaccinations at follow-up.
check.d: Credit any three of: GP review within a week of discharge, CXR at about 6 weeks, postpone/rebook the stress test, vaccination check. Alcohol advice is optional and not marked.

part2.lead: Mr Reid had a chest X-ray and blood tests at the imaging and pathology centre next door this morning and has come back to the practice this afternoon. Here are his observations, his chest X-ray report and his blood results.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains, Mr Reid asks, if not already covered:

  • "So is it COVID or not?"
  • "Do I really have to go back into hospital? I've only just got out."
  • "Did I catch this in the hospital?"
  • "What about my stress test next week?"

At first he is reluctant to go back to hospital. He agrees once the candidate explains, in plain words, that his oxygen level is falling and that the infection needs treatment in hospital. He is relieved to hear that the tests do not point to a blood clot, and that the hospital will also check his heart.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, on room air throughout. Weight 82 kg. The 14:30 and 14:45 sets were taken after he returned from imaging and pathology, seated at rest.
handover.model:
Read: at 10:15 he had a temperature of 38.6 °C, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air and BP 128/76, and was alert. Temperature 38.9 °C at 14:30 (not repeated at 14:45). At 14:30 and 14:45: HR 110 then 114, RR 24 then 26, SpO2 92% then 91% on room air, BP 122/72 then 120/70, still alert.

For Mr Reid: he is febrile, tachycardic and tachypnoeic, and his saturations are falling over the day. His blood pressure is preserved and he is not confused, so he is not shocked. RR is below 30 and SpO2 is above 90%, so CURB-65 scores no RR or BP points and CORB scores 0, but the trend is worsening.

What it changes: no adult observation chart applies in general practice, but these are abnormal and getting worse. He needs oxygen now (SpO2 below 92%, target 92 to 96%), repeat observations while he waits, and same-day transfer to hospital by ambulance. He is not safe to go home. Consider sepsis (infection with tachycardia, tachypnoea and new hypoxaemia); if ambulance transfer will be delayed, discuss giving the first antibiotic dose in the practice with the registrar (e.g. the first dose of amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally if he can swallow, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM if not, as agreed with the registrar).

rows.note: Back from imaging and pathology; coughing frequently
Repeat set by practice nurse; more breathless at rest; GP informed

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA and lateral, erect.

Clinical details: 68-year-old man with 2 days of cough with purulent sputum, fever and right pleuritic chest pain. Discharged from hospital 4 days ago after investigation of chest pain. Never smoker.

Comparison: PA chest X-ray at the local hospital 8 days ago (on admission), reported as normal.

Technique: adequate inspiration, not rotated, adequately exposed.

Findings:

  • Lungs: new airspace opacification in the right lower zone with air bronchograms. The right hemidiaphragm outline is lost, but the right heart border is preserved. On the lateral view the opacity projects posteriorly over the lower thoracic vertebrae, which appear denser lower down (spine sign). No cavity or air-fluid level. The left lung is clear. No nodule or mass.
  • Pleura: costophrenic angles sharp. No pleural effusion. No pneumothorax.
  • Heart and mediastinum: cardiothoracic ratio below 0.5. Mediastinum not widened. Hila normal. No upper lobe venous diversion, septal lines or interstitial oedema.
  • Diaphragm: left hemidiaphragm normal. No free gas under the diaphragm.
  • Bones and soft tissues: normal.
  • Lines and devices: none.

Conclusion: right lower lobe consolidation, new since 8 days ago, consistent with pneumonia in this clinical context. No effusion, cavitation or pulmonary oedema. A follow-up film after treatment is suggested to confirm resolution.
handover.model:
Spot diagnosis first: right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, new since a normal film 8 days ago.

Then systematically: PA and lateral erect, adequate technique. The right hemidiaphragm is obscured but the right heart border is preserved, which places the consolidation in the lower lobe, not the middle lobe; the spine sign on the lateral view confirms it. No cavity or fluid level, no effusion, no pneumothorax. Heart size normal with no pulmonary oedema. Mediastinum and hila normal. No mass.

For Mr Reid: this matches the right basal signs and the pleuritic pain. Consolidation that was not there on admission supports pneumonia acquired around his hospital stay. There is no cavitation to suggest an abscess despite the offensive sputum, and no effusion that might need draining. There is no oedema or cardiomegaly to suggest heart failure.

What it changes: it confirms pneumonia and gives a clear alternative to PE. He needs a follow-up film in about 6 weeks to make sure the consolidation has cleared.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected at 10:50, reported 13:40. No haemolysis. Discharge results from 4 days ago are shown in the notes.
handover.model:
Read: WCC 16.4 with neutrophils 13.9 (neutrophilia), up from 7.2 at discharge. CRP 168. Hb and platelets normal. Urea 8.4, above the range and above 7 mmol/L, up from 5.6, with a normal creatinine (94, eGFR 73). Sodium 136 and potassium normal. LFTs normal apart from albumin 33. D-dimer 0.58 mg/L FEU: above the standard cut-off of 0.50 but below his age-adjusted cut-off of 0.68.

For Mr Reid: marked inflammation with neutrophilia fits bacterial pneumonia. The urea rise with a normal creatinine suggests dehydration from fever and poor intake, and it scores a point on CURB-65 (total 2 with his age). Normal sodium and LFTs give no pointer to Legionella, though they do not exclude it. With a Wells score of 1.5 (HR over 100 only; PE unlikely), a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off excludes PE.

What it changes: he needs hospital care for moderate-severity pneumonia and IV fluids. A CTPA is not needed. Renal function allows standard antibiotic doses.

labs.title: Urea, electrolytes, creatinine and liver function tests

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Reid, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Reid now in general practice, and the plan you would expect once he is admitted.
Mr Reid asks you whether this is COVID and whether he really has to go back to hospital. What would you tell him, what warning signs would you give him, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student at the practice, calling with my supervising GP. Timothy Reid, 68.
  • Situation: right lower lobe pneumonia, febrile with SpO2 falling to 91% on room air. Requesting admission.
  • Background: discharged 4 days ago after a chest pain admission with normal investigations; stress test due next week. Two days of offensive purulent sputum, fevers and rigors, breathlessness, right pleuritic pain. Never smoker, no regular medicines, peanut anaphylaxis, no drug allergies.
  • Assessment: T 38.9, HR rising 104 to 114, RR 22 to 26, SpO2 94 to 91% on room air, BP 120/70, alert. X-ray: new RLL consolidation, no effusion or cavity, normal heart size, no oedema. WCC 16.4 (neutrophils 13.9), CRP 168, urea 8.4 (was 5.6), creatinine, sodium and LFTs normal. Wells 1.5 (HR over 100 only) with D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off, so PE excluded. CURB-65 2, CORB 0.
  • Recommendation: oxygen started, ambulance arranged. Please admit for cultures, viral PCR, antibiotics and fluids.

Most likely: right lower lobe bacterial pneumonia acquired around his hospital stay (hospital-acquired pneumonia). For it: started 2 days after discharge, offensive purulent sputum, fevers and rigors, pleuritic pain, right basal consolidation signs, neutrophilia, CRP 168, and new consolidation compared with 8 days ago.

  • Community-acquired or atypical pneumonia (e.g. Legionella): possible, but the recent admission is the more likely source. Normal sodium and LFTs and no diarrhoea, headache or exposures argue against Legionella.
  • PE: must be excluded after a hospital stay. Against it: mobile, had daily prophylactic anticoagulant injections, normal calves, Wells score of 1.5 (HR over 100 only) and a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off.
  • Heart failure or ACS: against it: no orthopnoea, oedema or frothy sputum, the pain is pleuritic, and the heart size is normal with no oedema. Not yet excluded: ECG and troponin in hospital.
  • Viral LRTI including COVID-19: against it: purulent sputum, lobar consolidation and neutrophilia. Swab still needed.
  • Aspiration or lung abscess: offensive sputum. Against it: no choking or blackouts, no cavity.

1. Immediate: sit him up. Oxygen by nasal prongs to SpO2 92 to 96%. Masks. Repeat observations every 15 minutes while waiting. Consider sepsis; if transfer is delayed, discuss a first antibiotic dose here with the registrar (e.g. amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM if he cannot swallow).
  2. Severity: CURB-65 of 2 (age 65 or over, urea above 7) is moderate. With falling SpO2, dehydration and the recent admission, he needs admission, not oral antibiotics at home.
  3. Disposition: discuss with the supervising GP. Phone the registrar or ED. Ambulance. Letter with the results and the discharge summary.
  4. In hospital: blood cultures x2, sputum culture and viral PCR without delaying antibiotics; ECG (and troponin in hospital); prompt empirical antibiotics per eTG hospital-acquired pneumonia: non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia on clinical judgement (no septic shock, no need for ventilatory or ICU support; CORB 0 supports this) with no multidrug-resistant organism risk (4-day stay, no recent antibiotics), so amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally 12-hourly (IV alternative per eTG if he cannot take oral); piperacillin+tazobactam IV is reserved for severe disease or multidrug-resistant risk; IV fluids; peanut allergy no restriction.
  5. No CTPA: PE is excluded.

• In plain words: an infection at the bottom of the right lung (pneumonia), probably picked up around his hospital stay. His oxygen is dropping, so he needs hospital for oxygen, a drip and antibiotics. Probably a few days. The blood test and his low clot risk mean a clot on the lung is very unlikely, and nothing so far points to his heart, but the hospital will check a heart tracing and blood test to be sure.
  • COVID: the tests point to a bacterial infection, but only a swab can rule COVID out. The hospital will test. Wear a mask and keep away from the grandchildren until the result is back.
  • Red flags: while waiting, tell the nurse or doctor straight away if he is more breathless, drowsy or has worse chest pain. After discharge, call 000 for worsening breathlessness, blue lips, new confusion or drowsiness, fainting, coughing up blood, or new or worse chest pain; see the GP the same day for returning fevers, not eating or drinking, or a cough not improving.
  • Follow-up: GP review within a week, CXR at 6 weeks, rebook stress test, vaccines.

ddx.dx: Hospital-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe, presenting after discharge
ddx.for: Sudden productive cough with offensive yellow sputum 2 days after discharge, fevers and rigors, right pleuritic pain, right basal consolidation signs, WCC 16.4 with neutrophilia, CRP 168, and right lower lobe consolidation that was not on the X-ray 8 days ago.
ddx.against: Symptoms began after he went home, so infection acquired in the community remains possible.

ddx.dx: Community-acquired pneumonia, including atypical pneumonia such as Legionella
ddx.for: Fever, purulent sputum, pleuritic pain and lobar consolidation in a 68-year-old.
ddx.against: The recent admission is the more likely source; normal sodium and LFTs, with no diarrhoea, headache, confusion or exposure to potting mix, spas or cooling towers, argue against Legionella.

ddx.for: Recent hospital admission, pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, tachycardia and falling saturations.
ddx.against: He walked daily and had daily prophylactic anticoagulant injections in hospital, has normal calves and no haemoptysis, has a Wells score of 1.5 (HR over 100 only) with a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off, and the X-ray shows a clear alternative.

ddx.dx: Acute left heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
ddx.for: Admitted for chest pain last week, now breathless and tachycardic.
ddx.against: No pink frothy sputum, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, pleuritic pain unlike the admission pain, ECG with sinus tachycardia and no acute ischaemic change, and normal heart size with no oedema on the X-ray; troponin still to be checked in hospital.

ddx.dx: Viral lower respiratory tract infection, including COVID-19 or influenza
ddx.for: Acute cough and fever after time in hospital; he is worried it is COVID.
ddx.against: Purulent offensive sputum, focal consolidation signs, neutrophilia and lobar consolidation point to bacterial pneumonia, though viral co-infection still needs testing.

ddx.dx: Aspiration pneumonia or early lung abscess
ddx.for: Offensive sputum, a dependent lower lobe, and nightly alcohol.
ddx.against: No choking, swallowing problems, vomiting or blackouts, and no cavity or air-fluid level on the X-ray.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Give the hospital admission only when the candidate asks about recent illness, hospital stays or tests; it is the key to the case. Mr Reid asks "Is this COVID?" near the end if his worries have not been explored. If the candidate says at the end of Part 1 that they would send him to ED now because he is febrile, tachycardic and has SpO2 94%, that is safe practice; say that the GP first sent him next door for urgent imaging and bloods, and go on with Part 2.

In Part 2 hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Mr Reid puts his questions during the explanation if the candidate has not covered them. The 14:45 observation set was taken before any oxygen was given. Credit items 24 to 28 wherever they appear in Part 2, in the ISBAR, the diagnosis or the management answer. The D-dimer is the trap: it is flagged high against the standard cut-off but is below his age-adjusted cut-off. A candidate who orders a CTPA without explaining why it is needed has not applied the pre-test probability.

A high-performing candidate characterises the sputum, finds the recent admission and the pneumonia symptoms, screens for PE, heart failure and the other causes, and examines the chest and both calves. In Part 2 they recognise new right lower lobe consolidation and use the Wells score and age-adjusted D-dimer to exclude PE. They calculate CURB-65 as 2, start oxygen to target and arrange admission by ambulance with a clear handover. They answer the COVID question honestly, postpone the stress test, and give specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic cough history and misses the hospital stay. They may send him home on oral antibiotics despite falling saturations, order a CTPA for a "positive" D-dimer, tell him it is definitely not COVID, or end with "come back if you're worse".
explain:
Diagnosis: pneumonia after a recent hospital stay

Mr Reid was discharged 4 days ago after investigations for chest pain. Two days later he developed a sudden productive cough with offensive yellow sputum, high fevers and rigors, severe malaise, breathlessness and right pleuritic chest pain. He has signs of consolidation at the right base. The X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation that was not there 8 days ago, with neutrophilia and a CRP of 168. This is bacterial pneumonia. Because it began so soon after discharge, it was probably acquired around the hospital stay (hospital-acquired pneumonia). Strictly, pneumonia with onset after discharge is community-acquired; because he was in hospital until 2 days before onset, many clinicians manage it as hospital-acquired so that hospital flora are covered. Choose with the admitting team and local guidance. That matters because hospital-acquired organisms can include Gram-negative bacteria and Staphylococcus aureus, which changes the choice of antibiotics. The recent admission is the single most important fact in the history, and it is only found if the candidate asks.

Approaching a cough

First sort a cough by its duration, then by whether it could be life-threatening:

  • Acute (under 3 weeks): URTI, acute bronchitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Life-threatening causes: heart failure, PE, pneumonia, exacerbation of COPD, inhalation injury.
  • Subacute (3 to 8 weeks): post-infectious cough, pneumonia, exacerbation of chronic bronchitis.
  • Chronic (over 8 weeks) in adults: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, GORD, chronic bronchitis, ACE inhibitor, emphysema, bronchiectasis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, lung cancer, TB, interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis.

For an acute cough, characterise the sputum. Purulent sputum suggests bacterial infection, and an offensive smell suggests anaerobes (aspiration, abscess). Haemoptysis raises PE, cancer or TB. Pink froth suggests pulmonary oedema. Then screen the associated systems: fever and rigors, breathlessness, pleuritic pain, heart failure symptoms, DVT symptoms and risk factors, and atypical features.

The differentials

  • Community-acquired pneumonia: the same clinical picture. Atypical organisms are suggested by headache, myalgia, diarrhoea, confusion, hyponatraemia or abnormal LFTs. In Australia, Legionella is linked to cooling towers, spas and potting mix.
  • Pulmonary embolism: must be excluded after any hospital stay. His Wells score is 1.5 (HR over 100 only), so PE is unlikely and a D-dimer is the right test. In patients over 50, an age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 µg/L, here 0.68 mg/L FEU) keeps the test sensitive and reduces unnecessary CTPAs. His result of 0.58 is above the standard cut-off but below the age-adjusted one, so PE is excluded. A chest X-ray cannot show or exclude PE; it is the low pre-test probability plus the D-dimer that excludes it. If PE were likely, a D-dimer would not be used and he would go straight to CTPA.
  • Left heart failure or ACS: important given last week's chest pain. Against them: no orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, oedema or frothy sputum, a pleuritic pain different from the admission pain, an ECG in the practice showing sinus tachycardia with no acute ischaemic change, and a normal heart size with no oedema on the X-ray. ACS is not excluded by these alone, so the hospital should repeat the ECG and check a troponin.
  • Viral LRTI including COVID-19 and influenza: cannot be excluded clinically, and co-infection occurs, so a respiratory viral PCR is part of the work-up.
  • Aspiration pneumonia or lung abscess: considered because of the offensive sputum and nightly alcohol. There is no history of choking or reduced consciousness, and no cavity on the X-ray.
  • URTI, acute bronchitis, COPD exacerbation, bronchiectasis, asthma: do not fit lobar consolidation, a never-smoker with no lung history, and no previous daily sputum.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: fever, rising heart and respiratory rates and saturations falling from 94% to 91% on room air, with BP preserved and no confusion. He is getting worse during the day.
  • Chest X-ray: loss of the right hemidiaphragm outline with a preserved right heart border places the consolidation in the right lower lobe; the spine sign on the lateral view confirms it. There is no effusion, cavity or oedema.
  • Bloods: neutrophilia and a high CRP support bacterial infection. Urea rising from 5.6 to 8.4 with a normal creatinine suggests dehydration, and a urea above 7 scores on CURB-65.

Severity and the decision to admit

CURB-65 (British Thoracic Society) gives one point each for new confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, RR 30 or more, low blood pressure (systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less) and age 65 or over. A score of 0 to 1 is low severity and can usually be treated at home. A score of 2 is moderate and warrants hospital care. A score of 3 or more is severe. In general practice without a urea, CRB-65 is used (Mr Reid: 1, for age). With his urea of 8.4, his CURB-65 is 2.

eTG assesses severity with CORB (acute confusion, oxygen saturation 90% or less, RR 30 or more, low blood pressure) or SMART-COP, together with clinical judgement. A CORB score of 2 or more indicates severe pneumonia. Mr Reid scores 0, so he does not have severe pneumonia now. SMART-COP is 3 (albumin below 35, SpO2 93% or less over 50): moderate, not severe. No score replaces judgement: his saturations are falling, he is dehydrated and febrile, and his pneumonia probably came from hospital, so he needs admission.

Management

  • In general practice: oxygen if SpO2 is below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96% in a patient without risk of hypercapnia (TSANZ). Repeat observations, phone the hospital team, transfer by ambulance, and send the results and discharge summary with him.
  • Consider sepsis: he has a source of infection with tachycardia, tachypnoea and new hypoxaemia. The ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard expects sepsis to be considered and antibiotics given promptly when it is suspected; if ambulance transfer will be delayed, discuss giving the first antibiotic dose in the practice with the registrar (e.g. the first dose of amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally if he can swallow, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM if not, as agreed with the registrar).
  • In hospital: blood cultures and sputum culture without delaying antibiotics; respiratory viral PCR; Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens; ECG and troponin. Start empirical antibiotics promptly, following eTG for hospital-acquired pneumonia. He has non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia on clinical judgement (no septic shock, no need for ventilatory or ICU support; CORB 0 supports this). For non-severe disease without risk factors for multidrug-resistant organisms, eTG recommends amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally 12-hourly (IV options if he cannot take oral). Mr Reid has no multidrug-resistant risk: his stay was short (4 days), he had no antibiotics in hospital, and he is not known to carry a resistant organism, so amoxicillin+clavulanate is the right choice for him. Severe disease or multidrug-resistant risk needs broader IV cover such as piperacillin+tazobactam. The admitting team modifies this according to cultures and progress. A peanut allergy does not restrict the choice of antibiotic.
  • Supportive care: IV fluids, paracetamol for fever and pleuritic pain, and VTE prophylaxis once admitted. Hand over his alcohol intake so that withdrawal can be monitored on the ward.
  • Postpone the stress test until he has recovered and let the cardiology team know.

Safety netting and follow-up

Explain the diagnosis in plain words and answer the COVID question honestly: the picture is of a bacterial chest infection, but only a swab can exclude COVID. He should wear a mask and keep away from the grandchildren until the result is back. Call 000 for worsening breathlessness, blue lips, confusion or drowsiness, fainting, coughing up blood, or new or worse chest pain. After discharge, see the GP within a week. A repeat chest X-ray at about 6 weeks is commonly arranged in older adults to confirm the consolidation has cleared and that nothing is hiding behind it. Rebook the stress test. Check his vaccinations, following the Australian Immunisation Handbook: influenza every year (funded from 65), COVID-19 as currently recommended, pneumococcal vaccine (funded at 70 for non-Indigenous adults), and recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix; funded from 65). RSV vaccine is recommended from 75, or from 60 with risk conditions. His 2 glasses of wine a night (about 3 standard drinks) exceed the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week.
points: Always ask about recent hospital stays in a patient with an acute cough: pneumonia starting soon after discharge may be hospital-acquired, and the stay is also a risk factor for PE.
Characterise the sputum: purulent sputum suggests bacterial infection, an offensive smell suggests anaerobes or aspiration, blood raises PE, cancer or TB, and pink froth suggests pulmonary oedema.
Use pre-test probability before a D-dimer. When PE is unlikely (Wells 4 or less), a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 µg/L over 50) excludes PE; when PE is likely, go straight to CTPA.
CURB-65 (confusion, urea above 7, RR 30 or more, low BP, age 65 or over) and eTG's CORB score guide where to treat, but a falling SpO2 and the clinical trend still decide admission.
Give oxygen when SpO2 is below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96%; in hospital, take cultures and a viral PCR, and start antibiotics without delay following the eTG hospital-acquired pneumonia guidance.
Safety-net with specific red flags and 000. Arrange GP follow-up, a repeat chest X-ray at about 6 weeks and a rebooked stress test, and check vaccinations.
